cards.note:
Australian bollards are white with a red reflector on the front and grey on the back.

Turkish bollards are similar but lack a back reflector. If unsure, check the sun position, landscape, or vegetation.

Austria's bollards are white with a black top and dark red or grey reflectors, often featuring a nipple-shaped black cap and sometimes a snow pole.

Slovenia’s bollards are similar but always have a white back reflector, whereas in Austria, white reflectors are rare but possible.
Blue Fortlev water tanks are often seen on Brazilian roofs.

The most common poles in Brazil resemble a ladder at the bottom. They are rectangular, with long segments at the base and small holes near the top. Chilean poles look similar but have 1–2 larger sections at the bottom instead of 3+ like Brazilian poles.

You might also find rounded concrete or wooden poles in Brazil, but they are less common and can be used for region-guessing within the country.
This diamond-shaped T-intersection "checkboard" sign is unique to Canada.
Canadian speed limit signs have the word "Maximum," while U.S. signs use "Speed Limit."
Stop signs with the word ‘Arret’ are unique to Quebec in Canada.

Chile uses square concrete poles with an indent on both sides. They are somewhat similar to Brazilian poles, however have fewer horizontal supports in the indent. The upper part typically has small pinholes.

Signposts in Colombia are made of white thin metal and have a distinct cross on the back.

In the photo, green checkmarks show the "real" Colombian cross, and red X's show the ones that aren't right.

In South America, yellow license plates are almost exclusive to Colombia. Commercial vehicles in Colombia may have white plates.

  • Images and descriptions courtesy of Plonkit.net
Bollards in Czechia have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back, with rarer blue and red variants. The same design is also found in Slovakia.
This signpost, where the pipe frame is bent around the sign, is unique to Denmark.

A Street View car with a white front and a roof rack filled with thick black rubber stripes is unique to the Dominican Republic. Only the capital Santo Domingo and the Northern city of Santiago de los Caballeros are covered.

With this landscape - similar cars can be found in Guatemala and Curaçao, but they lack the thick black stripes.

The French bollard is extremely recognizable and appears very often. It is a round white post with a pointed top and a reflector band going all the way around. The band can be grey or red. Some rare variations have a fully red top. A bollard that is commonly found in Scotland looks similar, but has a blunt top instead of a pointed one.

In France, these concrete ladder poles are pretty common. They're called "ladder" poles because of its similarity to the steps of a ladder.

NOTE: Spain can have the same poles, try using landscape or language to tell them apart.
The French word for street is “rue”. Street signs with "rue" can also be found in Belgium.

Germany uses these black and white bollards, with white and light-grey reflectors. The reflector will be orange on bollards next to intersections. They sometimes have plates containing the road number, and potentially other useful information. Many bollards also feature blue attachments on the side.

NOTE: Many European countries have similar bollards, however most will have different coloured reflectors. Luxembourg uses almost identical bollards, but they have 3 bolts instead of 2 on the reflector.

All regular road coverage in Ghana features a unique Google car with a visible roof rack and a piece of black tape on the right end of the front bar. The hood is usually visible, displaying a Street View car wrapping with a red rectangle and other distinctive elements.

The Greek language features a unique alphabet not used in any other language. It shares similarities with both the latin and cyrillic alphabet, however the lower case letters generally have softer shapes than the cyrillic letters.

This gray Street View car with a visible roof rack and mirrors is unique to Guatemala. Don’t confuse it with the Dominican Republic car, which has black stripes on the roof rack, or the Curaçao car, which has a black front. A similar car is found in Laos, so always check the surroundings before making a guess.

Concrete holey poles with medium-sized holes going all the way to the bottom are common. They are similar to those in Poland and Romania, but Polish poles have holes that don't go all the way to the top or bottom, and Romanian poles are usually wider and painted white at the bottom.
Iceland's yellow bollards with a white reflector are unique and extremely common, found on almost every section of rural road across the country.

Indonesian licence plates are black with white letters. The letters usually appear as three white sections through the blur.

Commercial vehicles use yellow licence plates.

Plates in newer coverage can be white too.

NOTE: Malaysian licence plates are also black, but generally have two white sections.
If you see cars with yellow front and back license plates in the Middle East, you are in Israel.

A short license plate with a double blue strip on the front and a long plate with a double blue strip on the back is unique to Italy. Similar long plates with a double blue strip can be found in Albania and France, but the front plates won’t be short.

While driving on the right side, yellow outer lines with white middle lines are commonly found in Jordan, Israel, and the UAE. The black back of the Google car without an antenna can help confirm you’re in Jordan 100%.

Kyrgyzstan can be recognized by the silver Google car with four visible bars. Coverage was done during winter, so trees often lack leaves, the landscape appears drab, and snow is visible in many areas.
This is a typical Malaysian directional sign. Green background and hexagonal yellow highway shields are unique to Malaysia.

Malaysian licence plates are black and generally have two white sections. These are visible even when blurred.

NOTE: Indonesian licence plates are also black, but they will have three white sections.
Berhenti stop signs are exclusive to Malaysia.

Gen4 Mongolia coverage was taken with two unique pickup trucks:

-White-Blue themed pickup truck mostly found only in Capital

-Pickup truck with a tent on top
The Street View car with a tent on top is unique to Mongolia. While Mongolia has other unique Google cars, this is the most common one.

If you see yellow license plates on both the front and back in Europe with a super flat landscape, it’s likely the Netherlands. Luxembourg also uses all-yellow plates but is much hillier. Denmark may have yellow plates for commercial vehicles, so use other clues like architecture, bike lanes, and surroundings to confirm it’s the Netherlands.
New Zealand has a unique white bollard with a red strip that wraps around the entire back and part of the front.
In Nigeria, Street View coverage often includes a police escort car visible "behind" the Street View car. However, it may sometimes be missing, so don’t rule out Nigeria if you don’t see it.

Polish bollards feature a red strip that wraps around the entire bollard, with a red reflector on the front (sometimes hard to see) and a white reflector on the back. They may also have numbers on them. (from Plonkit)
Holey poles with smaller holes are common in Poland. Similar poles can be found in Hungary and Romania, but in Poland, the holes don't extend all the way to the bottom or the top.

The Portuguese word for street is ‘Rua’.

NOTE: In Galician, the word for road is ‘Rúa’, with an accent on the ‘u’.

Qatar's landscape is predominantly desert, with arid, mostly flat expanses of sand as far as the eye can see. You will often not see many trees or other greenery.

The Google car will usually be blurred, with only the antenna on the left and a sliver of the car visible. Sometimes the entire white pickup truck can be visible.

You might occasionally confuse it with the UAE or Oman pickup truck coverage, but in those countries, the antenna on the pickup car will be in the middle.

Concrete holey poles with wide holes and usually painted white at the bottom are common in Romania. They are similar to poles in Poland and Hungary, but Polish poles have smaller holes that don’t go all the way to the bottom or top, and Hungarian poles typically have smaller holes as well.

White signposts painted black at the bottom are very common in both Russia and Kazakhstan. However, Kazakhstan's entire coverage was done with a pickup truck, making it easy to rule out, indicating you're in Russia.
Warnings are often written on the road in large letters, such as the famous “HUMP AHEAD”.
Slovakian bollards have orange double reflectors on the front and a single white reflector on the back, with rarer blue and red variants. The same design is also found in Czechia.

Slovenian bollards are white with a black top, featuring a bright red reflector on the front and a white reflector on the back.

Austria uses similar bollards, but the back reflector is usually black rather than white.

In South Africa, most paved roads have single yellow outer lines and white center lines. This can be used to differentiate from Australia which has only white lines and never single yellow lines.

REMEMBER:

  • The Middle East can also have single yellow outer lines, so use driving side to tell them apart (South Africa drives left)
  • Botswana, Eswatini and Lesotho also use single yellow outer lines (but they usually have a white car)
Korean script is highly distinctive, featuring a combination of circular shapes and blocky, straight-line characters.

Black and yellow diagonal stripes on poles are common in South Korea. You might confuse them with Taiwanese ones, but in South Korea, the stripes never go all the way to the bottom, while the ones in Taiwan usually do and have more of an orange tint to them.

In Spain, these concrete ladder poles can be found amongst other types. They're called "ladder" poles because of its similarity to the steps of a ladder.

NOTE: France can have the same poles, try using landscape or language to tell them apart.

Spanish pedestrian crossing signs have 8 stripes. This is the highest number of stripes in Europe, and almost unique to Spain.

NOTE: The only other European country with 8 stripes is Andorra.

Black and yellow diagonal stripes on poles are common. You might confuse them with South Korea's, but in Taiwan, they are usually longer, extend all the way to the bottom of the pole, and have an orange tint to them.

Square poles with small holes running from bottom to top are distinctive to Thailand. In Sri Lanka, similar poles exist, but the holes are limited to the top part of the pole.

Note: You can find same poles in Laos(but Laos drives right and most cities coverage is done with google car with roofrack)

Turkish bollards are white and rectangular with a red reflector on the front, making them quite unique. Similar bollards exist in Romania but are very rare. Australian bollards typically have a reflector on the back and a slightly different design(also they drive left in Australia/NZ comparing it to Turkey)
All stop signs in Turkey feature the text "DUR," making them unique to the country. No other country uses this stop sign.
Uganda's unique Google car is white with visible square mirrors, and its coverage is limited to Kampala. Some national parks in Uganda are covered with different cars, but these are quite rare.
If you have vibes/other clues that you are in the middle east and you have silver car in Gen3 that means you can only be in UAE.
In the UK, license plates are white on the front and yellow on the back. In Ireland, both the front and back plates are white.

cards.a: United States - No passing zone sign
cards.note: Yellow triangular signs with the text "No Passing Zone" are unique to the United States.
U.S. speed limit signs feature the text "Speed Limit," while Canadian signs use the text "Maximum."
Vietnam uses red-and-white striped signposts, and occasionally red-and-yellow ones.
